new.title: The Impact of a Magnetic Field on stochastically generated g-modes
new.summary: Magnetic fields have been proposed as a mechanism for suppressing low-frequency gravity modes in stellar interiors, providing a means of constraining internal magnetic field strengths. However, previous suppression criteria have largely relied on linear theory. Here, we use two-dimensional nonlinear magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations in a core convecting star to investigate the interaction of gravity waves with magnetic fields of varying strengths and geometries. Using both global and local field geometries, we find that amplitude reduction is gradual and frequency dependent, with low-frequency modes preferentially attenuated while higher-frequency modes can be amplified. In order to achieve significant suppression we require a magnetic field strength at least an order of magnitude larger than predicted by commonly used linear criteria. Its likely that this difference arises because magnetic fields can themselves excite waves through Maxwell stresses, offsetting magnetic attenuation. Our results demonstrate that strong magnetic modifications to wave propagation do not necessarily result in equivalent suppression of the global oscillation spectrum. The linear criteria typically used to infer field strengths based on mode suppression does not capture all relevant physics and should be used with care.

new.title: The chemical DNA of the Magellanic Clouds -- VII. The lithium abundance in the Small Magellanic Cloud and the discovery of 4 lithium-rich stars
new.summary: Measuring lithium abundance in galaxies beyond the Milky Way (MW) remains a challenging task. In these systems, only stars close to the tip of the red giant branch (RGB) are sufficiently bright to be observed this http URL A(Li) are expected to be altered by mixing episodes that occur during the stellar evolution, making the interpretation of measured abundances more complex. In this context, we present A(Li) of 209 RGB stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC),observed with FLAMES@VLT. Approximately one-third of the sample shows a Li line detected at a significance level above 5sigma, while about half of the sample has detections above 3sigma; for the remaining stars, only upper limits can be derived. This sample exhibits a significant star-to-star scatter in A(Li). Using theoretical models, we find that the observed scatter can be likely explained by the combination of 2 this http URL ,our stars span a wide range of ages, masses, [Fe/H]. Thermohaline mixing, one of the leading mechanisms proposed to explain the extra mixing occurring at the RGB bump, predicts different levels of A(Li) depletion depending on stellar mass and [Fe/H], naturally contributing to the observed scatter in A(Li). Second, in the SMC, the enrichment in A(Li) driven by novae is expected to occur at lower [Fe/H] than in the MW, because the SMC has experienced a lower star formation efficiency than the MW. This is also supported by the rise of A(Li) with decreasing age, as measured in 3 SMC globular clusters. Furthermore, we report the first identification of 4 low-mass Li-rich giant stars in the SMC, reinforcing the existence of Li-rich stars in extra-galactic systems. All these results demonstrate that A(Li) measured in stars close to the RGB tip, still provide valuable constraints on both stellar/galactic chemical evolution of A(Li) in external galaxies.

new.title: High-precision abundance analysis of a unique CEMP-no star in Sculptor
new.summary: The Carbon-Enhanced Metal-Poor stars (CEMP-no, low barium) are commonly accepted as the direct descendants of Population III (Pop III) stars which either ended their lives as faint supernovae (SNe; E_SN < 10^51 erg) or were fast-rotating stars (spinstars). While CEMP-no stars are common in the Milky Way (MW) and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), they are surprisingly rare in dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs). This could hide an environmental dependence of the properties of Pop III stars, highlighting the importance of high-resolution studies of CEMP-no stars in dSphs. Here we present the first detailed study of a CEMP-no star with [Fe/H] < -3 in the Sculptor dSph. The high-resolution VLT/UVES spectra allowed us to derive one of the most precise abundance patterns obtained for a star belonging to a dwarf galaxy, providing chemical abundances for 17 elements and 4 upper limits. This star, DR20080, is extremely metal-poor, [Fe/H] = -3.26, and clearly enhanced in carbon, [C/Fe] = +1.60 (after correcting for internal mixing). Furthermore, it has low [Ba/Fe] = -1.28. The oxygen abundance of DR20080 ([O/Fe] = +1.53) is significantly higher than the average found in CEMP-no stars in the MW, while the iron-peak elements are under-abundant ([Mn/Fe] = -1.02; [Ni/Fe] = -0.45). The abundance pattern of DR20080 was compared to theoretical yield predictions of Pop III and Pop II SNe to infer the properties of its progenitor. The best result points toward a double Pop III progenitor scenario, with the major contributor to the abundance pattern being a Pop III faint SN with mass m_PopIII = 43 M_0 and explosion energy E_SN = 0.6 x 10^51 erg, while the minor contributor is a Pop III hypernova of m_PopIII = 19.4 M_0 and E_SN = 10 x 10^51 erg. The unique properties of DR20080 have never before been observed in Sculptor or in any other environment within the MW and its satellite system.

new.title: Signatures of mass transfer in open-cluster blue straggler stars. I. Collinder 261: Evidence from rotation, binarity, and chemical abundances
new.summary: We present the first dedicated $v\sin i$ survey of blue straggler stars (BSS) in the old open cluster Collinder 261 ($t=6.7$ Gyr), based on VLT/FLAMES-GIRAFFE spectroscopy of 40 BSS and 42 turn-off/subgiant (TO/SGB) reference stars. Seventeen of the 39 BSS entering the statistics (44%) rotate faster than 40 km/s, whereas all TO/SGB reference stars are slow rotators; fast rotation is strongly linked to spectroscopic binarity. TESS light curves identify seven eclipsing or ellipsoidal binaries with $P_{orb}=0.5$-2.1 d, all rotating at the velocity set by tidal synchronisation, so in these systems the fast rotation is maintained by a close post-mass-transfer orbit and does not date the formation event. Differential C, O, Ba, and Fe abundances for the 22 slow rotators reveal that 62% carry the surface-pollution signature of mass transfer, in two distinct patterns separated by an empty ~1 dex gap in [Ba/Fe]: a Ba-rich group tracing AGB donors and a C/O-enhanced, Ba-normal group tracing donors below the $s$-process activation mass. The BSS iron abundance is consistent with the cluster value; the few apparent Fe excesses are partly explained by differential reddening and do not affect the abundance pattern. The correlated C-O enrichment is opposite to the depletion seen in globular-cluster BSS, indicating binaries wide enough for donors to reach the AGB. With $A^+_{r_h}=0.171\pm0.034$ and $f_{FR-BSS}=44\pm8$%, Collinder 261 extends the globular-cluster rotation-density trends into the open-cluster regime: its BSS were assembled by a continuously operating binary channel, and their chemistry records the dynamical environment of the host cluster.

new.title: Planetary material is a major source of hydrogen in helium-atmosphere white dwarfs
new.summary: Many white dwarfs with helium-dominated atmospheres show traces of hydrogen in their spectra. On average, the total mass of hydrogen within their convective envelopes increases with age, but there is no consensus on the origin of such hydrogen. Hypotheses include upward diffusion from hidden reservoirs deep within the envelope, or accretion, alongside heavier elements, of planetary material. We construct a simple model that includes both pathways, and test it using two independent samples of helium-atmosphere DB white dwarfs from the DESI and SDSS spectroscopic surveys, selected to have Gaia colours BP-RP > -0.25, corresponding roughly to 10000 < $T_{\rm eff}$ < 19000K. We find that at least $22 \pm 2$ per cent of the helium-atmosphere white dwarfs with detectable hydrogen must have accreted some of it from their planetary systems, via ices, hydrated minerals or atmospheres. We thus demonstrate that planetary hydrogen is a necessary ingredient to explain the spectral evolution of white dwarfs as a population, rather than only extreme hydrogen-enriched cases.

new.title: Near-Ultraviolet and Optical Observations of the White Dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 Reveal Variable Periodicity in its Transiting Debris System
new.summary: We observed the transiting debris disk system around the white dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 using the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in 2025 October, obtaining near-ultraviolet (NUV) spectroscopy with STIS over five consecutive HST orbits. Our abundance analysis supports the accretion of a chondritic body. We complemented our HST program with 16 days of optical time-series photometry beginning in 2025 October, which reveal variable periodicity and rapidly evolving transit morphology. Previous monitoring by TESS during Sectors 4 and 31 confirmed a predominant, stable transit orbital period, $P_{\rm A} = 9.937$ hr, along with a second, transient period, $P_{\rm B} = 11.2$ hr. Our 2025 autumn light curves show transits are dominated by $P_{\rm B} = 11.17$ hr with $P_{\rm A}$ initially appearing as a weaker, secondary feature and eventually returning to predominance. We also identify a candidate transit period of 7.64 hr during the final days of the 2025 autumn campaign, although its significance and persistence remain uncertain. We add simultaneous $ugr$ light curves collected with ULTRACAM in 2024 November that are dominated by $P_{\rm A}$ and show no significant color term. We further compare the transit depths in optical photometry concurrent with our NUV observations, again measuring a lack of transit-dependent extinction except during the fifth HST orbit where a reddening term may arise. The observed variable periodicity and potentially changing color behavior illuminate ongoing dynamical processes, namely collisions, and demonstrate the opportunity for studying dust physics in real time at white dwarf debris disks.

new.title: Identification of chromospheric dynamical signatures in the 2022 December 27 solar flare with DKIST
new.summary: Spectroscopic observations by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) with unprecedented capabilities provide new insights into the evolving fine structure in the chromosphere during solar flares. We analyzed Ca II 8542Å spectra, formed in the middle chromosphere, of a minor flare observed by DKIST's Visible Spectropolarimeter in a single raster lasting 1.5 hours. We characterized the dynamic features in the spectra, then identified the spatial scales and context of these features during the evolution of flare heating. To do so, we developed a multi-layer, hierarchical clustering algorithm, with which 17,422 line profiles of flaring spectra were characterized into 19 clusters of similar spectral features. We then examined the spatial structure of the spectral clusters and also the time when the spectra were observed with respect to the local heating history inferred from observations by the Atmosphere Imaging Assembly. The spectral clusters form a set of spatially coherent structures, comprised of a central kernel with an enveloping halo. The smallest kernel size that is identified has a width of $\le 400$ km. Furthermore, spectral clusters in the pore and plage exhibit distinct properties such as kernel size, line shift, and spatial variation, which may be a result of different background atmosphere, and may also reflect different stage of local heating. High-resolution observations with improved cadence can further our understanding of the evolution of chromospheric fine structure.

new.title: Understanding Coronal `Seeing' using High Angular Resolution Radio Observations of Active Solar Emissions
new.summary: Solar radio bursts are generated through the plasma emission mechanism by beams of accelerated electrons travelling along magnetic field lines. They serve as powerful probes of the ambient coronal plasma and magnetic fields. At low frequencies, however, propagation through the turbulent, magnetised coronal plasma strongly modifies their observed properties. Disentangling these propagation effects from the intrinsic nature of the emission therefore remains a major challenge. Despite the long history of observations, there are only a few that leverage high-angular-resolution imaging. This is primarily due to the prevailing expectations that scattering from coronal density inhomogeneities significantly increases the apparent source size, obscuring any fine-scale structures that might be present. While small-scale features are routinely observed in EUV and X-rays, few are detected at meter wavelengths. Numerous studies have focused on quantifying the effect of scattering on the observed apparent size of a point solar radio source. Naturally, their results vary significantly depending on the specifics of the model used to describe coronal inhomogeneities and the scattering prescription applied -- ranging from sub-arcseconds to arcminutes. Recent high angular resolution observations with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) -pathfinders, uGMRT and LOFAR, have revealed unexpectedly compact sources, with sizes as small as $\sim9$ arcseconds in type-I noise storms. Forthcoming high-fidelity and angular resolution SKAO observations will transform our understanding of solar radio emissions by constraining scattering models, improving coronal diagnostics, and revealing fine structures crucial for understanding solar radio emissions and propagation effects.

new.title: Thermal-pulse-resolved Binary Population Synthesis with Detailed Stellar Models: Implications for Long-period WD+MS Formation
new.summary: The origin of the long-orbital-period white dwarf--main-sequence (WD+MS) binaries revealed by Gaia challenges the traditional association of common-envelope evolution (CEE) with short orbital periods. We develop a thermal-pulse-resolved binary population synthesis framework based on 51 detailed MESA evolutionary tracks with initial masses of 1--6 $M_{\odot}$. Applying these tracks to $5\times10^6$ initially sampled binaries, we follow the time-dependent stellar radius, wind mass loss, angular momentum, and tidal interactions, while calculating the envelope binding energy directly from the donor structure at the onset of Roche-lobe overflow. We find that thermal pulses can trigger binary interaction through envelope expansion and tidal orbital shrinkage, while the weakly bound envelopes of highly evolved thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch (TP-AGB) donors allow CE ejection with limited orbital contraction. For our standard model, with $\alpha_{\mathrm{CE}}$ = 0.3 and $\alpha_{\mathrm{th}}$ = 0.5, systems with orbital periods above 30 days constitute approximately 11.5\% of the resulting TP-AGB-initiated post-CE binaries (PCEBs). Long-period PCEBs can form across a large range of CE parameters and can reach periods of several hundred days even without any internal-energy contribution when $\alpha_{\mathrm{CE}}$ = 1. Their WD masses peak near 0.6 $M_\odot$, whereas systems containing more massive WDs are rare. Moreover, long-period PCEBs closely follow the single-star initial--final mass relation, providing a potential diagnostic of their formation channel in clusters, where progenitor masses can be independently constrained. Our results identify late TP-AGB CEE as a viable contributor to the observed long-period WD+MS population.

new.title: Asteroseismology of the Gaia SB2 HD 70510: From Radial Modes to Component Masses
new.summary: Double-lined spectroscopic binary (SB2) orbits give mass ratios and projected component masses, but the absolute masses depend on the unknown inclination. HD 70510 is a Gaia DR3 SB2 in which regular $\delta$ Scuti pulsations constrain the properties of one component. We analyze nine sectors of TESS photometry and combine stellar evolution and pulsation modelling with a two-star spectral energy distribution (SED) fit to the unresolved Gaia and 2MASS photometry. Five high-signal-to-noise peaks form a sequence consistent with the radial fundamental mode and four consecutive overtones. Two stable pulsation clocks show the sign and amplitude expected from the orbital motion of the Gaia primary, identifying it as the pulsator. Combining the radial-mode and binary-SED fits with the Gaia SB2 orbit gives $M_1=1.594^{+0.026}_{-0.026}\,M_\odot$, $R_1=1.482^{+0.014}_{-0.012}\,R_\odot$, and an age of $171^{+112}_{-99}$ Myr. We obtain an orbital inclination of $i=82.1^{+3.5}_{-3.4}$ deg and a companion mass of $M_2=1.121^{+0.029}_{-0.028}\,M_\odot$. These intervals are statistical and remain conditional on the adopted radial-mode identification and stellar and binary-SED models. The primary lies close to the zero-age main sequence, while the roughly 6000-K companion contributes 14-28% of the unresolved optical-to-near-infrared flux. HD 70510 shows how regular pulsations can provide component masses for non-eclipsing TESS binaries with Gaia DR3 SB2 orbital solutions.

new.title: Angular momentum transport in a newborn protostar--disc system: magnetic braking, spiral arms and the magneto-rotational instability
new.summary: Angular momentum transport in young protostar--disc systems involves magnetic braking, magneto-rotational turbulence and gravitational instability, mechanisms that are usually studied separately and on different scales. We present a three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic simulation, including Ohmic and ambipolar diffusion, that follows the collapse of a $1~M_\odot$ dense core continuously from the cloud scale to the formation of the protostar, and then the resulting protostar--disc system for $\sim 64~\mathrm{yr}$ at a resolution of $\sim 10^{-4}~\mathrm{AU}$ at the protostellar surface. We decompose the azimuthally averaged angular momentum budget into Reynolds, Maxwell and gravitational torques, each split into a radial and a meridional component, over a quasi-steady phase of the evolution. The collapse produces a thick disc an order of magnitude more massive than the protostar, whose specific angular momentum decreases as it accretes. Accretion through the disc is vertically layered, with accreting and decreting layers at the same radius, a pattern set layer by layer by the torques. The transport separates into three regimes delimited by the coupling of the magnetic field to the gas. Magnetic braking operates in the envelope. Maxwell stresses dominate inside $\sim 0.1~\mathrm{AU}$, where the field recouples and the magneto-rotational instability develops. In the ambipolar dead zone that makes up the bulk of the disc, the Reynolds stress dominates, carried by $m=2$ spiral arms in a marginally unstable disc, with the gravitational stress as a secondary contributor. Meridional transport is as important as radial transport, so that a one-dimensional viscous model fitted to the net mass flux would require a negative $\alpha$ over part of the disc.

new.title: Towards a new model of the compact triple system $λ$ Tauri I. Improved periods and preliminary elements of the triple system
new.summary: We analysed our new radial velocity measurements and photometric observations (covering a time interval of 46838~days and 39100~days, respectively) as well as those from previous studies to derive accurate ephemerides for both orbits of the compact triple system $\lambda$ Tau. In the case of the inner eclipsing subsystem, we obtained a~linear ephemeris of T min.I=HJD 2440998.86069(35)+3.952952845(81)xE, improving the accuracy of the previous solutions by more than an order of magnitude. This allowed us to reproduce well all available light curve minima, including the first one recorded in 1844. Furthermore, the period of the outer subsystem, determined from radial velocity analysis, appears to be constant over the interval of available observations, with the corresponding linear ephemeris being T periast.=HJD 2456822.5(3.6)+33.02480(28)xE. Assuming near coplanarity of the inner and outer orbits, we estimated the preliminary physical properties of the whole system. We found that the secondary of the inner subsystem is filling or nearly filling its Roche lobe. We used the long-term stability of the eclipsing subsystem period to place a strong upper limit on the rate of the proposed episodic mass transfer to its primary component. Our results constitute a preparatory step for a follow-up study that will also include an analysis of a rich collection of optical spectro-interferometric observations and use a full-fledged numerical model to describe the evolution of the orbital architecture of the system. Particular attention will be focused on determining the inner orbit forced eccentricity and understanding the absence of the apsidal advance of the outer orbit in our present solution.

new.title: Constraining electron heat flux from reduced measurements
new.summary: Coronal heating estimates depend partly on electron heat transport. Different electron velocity distributions can match the same observations yet carry different heat fluxes. We ask which measurements are enough to determine heat flux without finding how electrons are distributed across all speeds and directions. The solar wind carries electrons outward from the corona and allows their velocities to be measured directly. Using one Wind measurement, we keep density, mean flow, temperature and angular summaries for each energy channel. In the fixed-bin model, electron distributions that match these quantities have heat fluxes from 3.58 to 19.85 $\mu$W m$^{-2}$. Keeping the correlation between electron motion along and across the magnetic field fixes the heat flux at 11.73 $\mu$W m$^{-2}$, matching the original bin calculation. This recovers heat flux without reconstructing the full shape of the electron velocity distribution. When the measured counts vary, retaining the required correlations leaves the same heat-flux range as direct calculation from those counts. We propose testing coronal observations in the same way to find which features of electron motion they constrain well enough to determine heat transport. Those constraints could help establish the heating requirements used to assess coronal heating mechanisms.

new.title: Revisiting the centrifugal breakout scaling relationship for H$α$ emission in light of $ρ$ Oph C, the coolest B-type star with an H$α$-bright centrifugal magnetosphere
new.summary: The corotating magnetospheres of B-type stars are strongly affected by magnetic field strength and rotational velocity, which determine both the geometry and strength of visible and radio emission; however, H$\alpha$ emission largely disappears below a bolometric luminosity of $\log{(L / L_\odot)} \sim 2.8$. The nearby B5 V star $\rho$ Oph C (HD 147932) is the least-luminous rapidly rotating magnetic B-type star to display magnetospheric H$\alpha$ emission. While $\rho$ Oph C's radio magnetosphere has been extensively studied, its magnetic field and H$\alpha$ magnetosphere have been constrained only via snapshot observations. We present a new dataset of high-resolution ESPaDOnS spectropolarimetry covering the star's rotational period, which is revisited by combining Hipparcos, K2 and TESS photometry. We find that the star's magnetic field strength and geometry are consistent with the model inferred from radio data. As expected from the magnetic model, there is very little variability in H$\alpha$. Comparison of the light curve to both equivalent width measurements from metallic lines and magnetospheric models suggests that the star's photometric variability is dominated by surface chemical abundance spots; however, there is complex rotationally modulated variability at about the mmag level which probably originates in the magnetosphere. $\rho$ Oph C is the least luminous B-type star in which magnetospheric H$\alpha$ emission has yet been detected, and its emission is notably weaker than the predictions of the centrifugal breakout model. Its photometric eclipse depth is also much lower than predicted by the CBO model. However, its radio luminosity is consistent with CBO predictions. We speculate on this basis that $\rho$ Oph C may be a transitional object between effective temperature regimes with hydrogen-dominated and decoupled metallic winds.

cross.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
cross.summary: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.

cross.title: ExoPlanetLab: Bayesian orbit fitting of Gaia-DR4 epoch astrometry, radial velocities and relative astrometry
cross.summary: Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) provides epoch astrometry from which thousands of giant planets and many substellar and stellar companions can be characterised. We present ExoPlanetLab, an open-source package for Bayesian orbit inference from Gaia epoch astrometry, radial velocities (RVs) and relative astrometry, validated on simulated and real data. The model orbit is compared with the epoch residuals after removing the part absorbed by the single-star fit. A Student-t likelihood describes heavy-tailed data. A robust Keplerian periodogram with bootstrap false-alarm probabilities gives starting values for a joint fit. Five samplers are available: tempered ensemble MCMC, two nested samplers and two reversible-jump samplers. Evidences for a fixed number of companions select that number. Acceleration and scan-angle models test whether an orbit is warranted. The samplers agree within 0.1 sigma on a simulated two-planet system. In 180 injections all fits converge, and all signals with signal-to-noise ratio S >= 10 are detected. The posteriors show no significant bias, but the period coverage is below nominal: 90% of the true periods lie within their 95% credible intervals. None of 30 companion-free data sets gives a false detection. On DR4 pre-release data the orbit of Gaia BH3 is recovered within 1.4 sigma of published solutions. The Student-t model brings the astrometric period and eccentricity of HD 114762 onto its RV orbit. Eight simulated relative positions narrow the period's credible interval to 0.27 of its width, and Octofitter agrees within 0.2 sigma on the same data. The code is validated for single sources with DR4-like epoch astrometry, with or without RVs. Relative astrometry is tested on simulated data only. The main limits are an uncorrelated noise model and the computing cost, which grows linearly with the number of measurements and steeply with the number of companions.

cross.title: Response of Circular Binaries to Monochromatic Gravitational Waves
cross.summary: The exchange in specific orbital energy between a test particle in a Keplerian binary orbit and a continuously incident linearized gravitational wave (GW) is considered. Analytical expressions for the rate of change of energy, semi-major axis and mean motion of the test particle are derived. Numerical solutions illustrate a resonance effect betwen the GWs frequency and the particle's initial orbital frequency. We distinguish between bounded short-period oscillations and resonant libration. The effect of the GWs angle of incidence with the particle's orbital plane is also considered. Using an illustrative high GW strain we show that changes to the eccentricity are bounded while inclination exhibits small linear growth for an initially flat, circular orbit. Long coherence requirements linit the observational significance of GW resonance to astrophysical systems with very short orbital periods.

cross.title: r-Process Abundance Variations in Globular Clusters as Fossils of Turbulent Mixing
cross.summary: Several metal-poor Galactic globular clusters exhibit substantial star-to-star $r$-process abundance variations at nearly fixed [Fe/H], with the ensemble suggesting smaller variations toward increasing metallicity. We investigate whether this chemical structure can be inherited from incomplete mixing in the galactic environments in which the clusters formed. Using parsec-scale simulations of rare-element transport in a supernova-driven turbulent disk, we follow the redistribution of $r$-process ejecta and characterize the abundance structure of gas selected to trace star-forming environments. Rare enrichment events generate strong [Eu/Fe] inhomogeneities that persist across a range of physical scales. As chemical evolution proceeds, the available abundance variance decreases, while spatial averaging over larger regions reduces the differences between their characteristic abundances. The simulations provide substantial pre-collapse $r$-process variance at low [Fe/H] and show the same broad decline toward higher metallicity suggested by the globular-cluster measurements. Our results support an interpretation in which at least some of the observed $r$-process variations are inherited from pre-existing chemical structure in the natal environment, allowing globular clusters to preserve a fossil record of the mixing history between rare enrichment and star formation.

repl.title: Is the Quiet-Sun Heating Requirement Observationally Established?
repl.summary: How much energy does the quiet corona require? Its radiation shows that energy must be supplied. Electrons also carry heat into or out of it. We ask whether temperature observations justify the heat-flow estimate used to judge a heating mechanism's energy supply. Two radio methods give temperatures near 0.62 and 1.5 million kelvin. A population with extra fast electrons can give both readings. Unresolved structure and delayed ion formation also leave Maxwellian explanations open. Neither temperature interpretation alone determines the heat flow. The tested local conduction formula diverges for the idealized fast-electron model with an unbroken tail. Applying X-ray limits to the model still leaves about 5--6% of the electrons holding 28--33% of its kinetic energy. The heat they carry depends on the balance between directions and on conditions along their paths. Source and collision calculations test whether the population could be sustained. The observations examined here do not establish whether the conductive estimate is accurate enough for the heating comparison. We cannot judge whether a mechanism supplies enough energy against a heat loss we have not established. Measuring, reliably calculating, or sufficiently bounding that loss would settle this part of the budget.

repl.title: Tight asteroseismic upper limits on hot subdwarf magnetism
repl.summary: The apparent absence of magnetism in subdwarf B stars (sdBs) has emerged as an outstanding observational puzzle, especially in light of their likely origin in binary interactions. Gravity-mode pulsations in some sdBs offer a unique opportunity to extend recent successes in asteroseismic magnetic field detection in red giants. In the presence of strong magnetic fields, gravity modes are expected to be significantly damped, suppressing their observed amplitudes. We place stringent upper limits on magnetic fields in 30 hot subdwarfs by using the observation of low-frequency dipole and quadrupole modes to rule out magnetic suppression. Even under conservative assumptions, our upper limits constrain near-surface magnetic fields to below a kilogauss in roughly half of our sample, with the strongest individual constraint reaching down to $\sim20\,\mathrm{G}$. These upper limits reinforce the apparent dearth of magnetic fields in hot subdwarfs and demonstrate asteroseismology as a powerful new probe of magnetism in these stars.

repl.title: Slowly rotating white dwarfs in f (R, T ) = R + 2λT gravity: structure and stationary tidal response
repl.summary: We calculate the structure and stationary tidal response of cold carbon fluid white dwarfs in $f(R,T)=R+2\lambda T$ gravity through second order in uniform rotation. Equilibria are compared at fixed baryon number, with angular momentum also conserved during each aligned electric quadrupolar tidal perturbation. Negative coupling increases radii and dimensional tidal deformabilities over the common mass range. For the baryon sequence studied, background readjustment accounts for 95.8--97.5\% of the rotational enhancement at 40\% of each model's Kepler reference frequency. The explicit mixed rotational tidal contribution is positive and numerically resolved, but subdominant. At that spin, the enhancement relative to each coupling's static model decreases from 107.4\% in general relativity to 14.2\% at the most negative coupling, despite its larger absolute deformability. This reduction reflects less relative background expansion and a different Love-number variation.

repl.title: Pair Space Analysis of Some Four-Body Central Configurations
repl.summary: I study central configurations in the four-body problem, i.e., configurations in which the forces on all the bodies point to a fixed, single point in space. The newly formulated pair-space formalism yields a set of vectorial equations that fully characterize such configurations. I investigate a sub-class of solutions in which at least two pairs of inter-body distances are equal. The only such non-collinear configurations are the tetrahedron (the unique non-planar configuration), kites and the isosceles trapezium. The specific shapes (internal angles) are determined by the ratio of the masses of the bodies. Mathematical expressions are given for all these relations.

repl.title: Heavy-element dust as an explanation for the late-time kilonova spectra
repl.summary: Neutron star mergers are a leading site of r-process, producing radioactively powered optical and infrared transients known as kilonovae. Observations of the kilonovae AT2017gfo, associated with the gravitational-wave event GW170817, and AT2023vfi, associated with GRB 230307A, have enabled measurements of the mass of ejected r-process material and identification of heavy elements in the ejecta. However, late-time observations reveal strong infrared emission with temperature below 1000 K, which is difficult to explain by atomic absorption and emission processes alone. In this paper, we propose that kilonova ejecta provide conditions favorable for the formation of dust grains composed of refractory r-process elements including Zr, W, and Os. Assuming a simplified, empirically derived single power-law temperature evolution and using W reaction rate coefficients as a proxy, our kinetic dust formation calculations indicate that dust could form efficiently, particularly in slow ejecta. This stands in contrast to a previous study that relied on a classical nucleation framework. By performing radiative transfer simulations that incorporate dust formation, we demonstrate that, if formed, r-process dust could naturally explain the observed late-time infrared emission, although refining ejecta parameters and geometry will be necessary to match specific observational cases. The formation and abundance of r-process dust are highly sensitive to ejecta mass, composition, and expansion velocity. Infrared emission from r-process dust may therefore potentially serve a new probe of heavy-element production in neutron star mergers.

repl.title: Breaking the AGB Color Degeneracy with Variability and H$_2$O: A Consistent Picture of AGB Chemistry, Dust, and the J-Region Across Environments
repl.summary: Resolved asymptotic giant branch (AGB) populations present many observational puzzles. We consider three often treated separately: photometric C/O classification boundaries must be redrawn empirically in new environments; hydrostatic model grids are too blue in bands sampling H2O absorption; and J-region (JAGB) luminosities can differ between fields of a single galaxy. Pulsation connects them into a coherent picture. Using SPHEREx spectroscopy of AGB stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) with JWST/NIRCam photometry and HST time-series of the SN Ia host M101, placed on a common scale by synthetic photometry, we investigate how AGB variability, surface chemistry, and circumstellar dust depend on environment. We develop an F182M index sensitive to 1.9$\mu$m H2O absorption that chemically classifies variable AGB stars and reveals oxygen-rich (O-rich) stars degenerate with carbon-rich (C-rich) stars in broadband colors. Because these features arise in extended atmospheric layers, hydrostatic grids struggle to reproduce them. Pulsation and circumstellar dust are asymmetrically linked: nearly all stars with substantial infrared excess are variable, while many variables show little dust. This supports mass loss initiated by pulsation and enhanced by dust formation. Variable O-rich AGB stars in M101 are up to ~0.7 mag redder than their LMC counterparts in dust-sensitive colors, consistent with more efficient silicate-dust production at higher metallicity, while C-rich populations depend less on environment. Color windows that select C-rich stars cleanly in the LMC are therefore 33-68% O-rich in the metal-rich M101. This challenges the J-region's universality as a standard candle while evading standard self-consistency checks. We recommend combining variability, or the infrared excess that implies it, with photometry of molecular features to improve AGB classification at 0.75-5.0$\mu$m.

repl.summary: We investigate the equilibrium structure and stability against radial oscillations of a variety of two-fluid compact objects containing ordinary baryonic matter admixed with cold dark matter coupled through the background spacetime. For the ordinary fluid, we employ a QCD equation of state compatible with chiral effective field theory at nuclear densities (supplemented by the BPS and Negele-Vautherin models at extremely low densities) and with perturbative QCD in the high-density regime while also satisfying also current astrophysical data. For the dark fluid, we assume self-interacting fermionic matter with particle masses of $m_f=$ 2, 5, 10, and 100 GeV and two self-interaction strengths of $y=0.1$ and $10^3$. By scanning a large range of central pressures for both fluids, we identify the presence of dark compact planets, dark white dwarfs, dark neutron stars and the so-called dark oysters. Importantly, these objects are not only in two-fluid hydrostatic equilibrium, but they are also stable against two-fluid radial oscillations. We find that the relative representation of each class in the radially stable sample is strongly sensitive to the combinations of $m_f$ and $y$, with some combinations entirely suppressing some of these object classes within the sampled domain while favoring others. In addition to these classes, strong self-repulsion supports stable, dark-matter-dominated branches with compact ordinary-matter cores and extended dark halos, approaching the self-interacting fermion-star limit. Finally, we calculate the gravitational redshift at the ordinary-matter surface, $z_{\rm OM}$, including the contribution of extended dark-matter halos for which we found radially stable configurations with $z_{\rm OM}>2$.

repl.title: The Brown Dwarf Desert is a Mass-Ratio Desert: Astrometric Demographics of 63,254 Stars
repl.summary: Brown dwarfs are rare as close companions to stars compared to planets and stellar companions, a paucity known as the brown dwarf desert. Whether the desert sits at a fixed companion mass or a fixed companion-to-star mass-ratio $q$ has been difficult to test, because microlensing, radial velocities, and direct imaging have sampled comparatively narrow slices of stellar mass and separation. Here we apply a novel joint-modelling method to Hipparcos and Gaia DR2/DR3 astrometry from 63,254 stars to complete this picture with a sample 1-2 orders of magnitude larger than those of previous wide-orbit demographic studies. For the first time, we present a single survey that measures occurrence rates of both planetary and stellar companions on 3--94 yr orbits ($\sim$2--20\,au) across host masses from M dwarfs to B stars. We find that the desert is a mass-ratio feature: companions are strongly depleted at $q\approx2\%$ independent of stellar mass from M to B stars, and a desert at fixed companion mass is excluded. Furthermore, we find a positive trend in occurrence with metallicity below the mass-ratio desert, but a negative trend above. The desert therefore separates two distinct populations, plausibly two formation channels, that each scale with stellar mass: the lightest stellar-like companions of K stars ($\sim13 \, M_{jup}$) are less massive than the heaviest planet-like companions of B stars ($\sim27, M_{jup}$), which continue well beyond the deuterium-burning limit. Mass-ratio, not mass, is therefore the physically meaningful boundary between planets and their stellar-like counterparts.
